analysis.one_liner: Lets cities and towns build their own public broadband networks even where state laws ban them.
analysis.headline: The Community Broadband Act cleared a Senate committee with bipartisan support and was placed on the Senate calendar, but it never got a Senate vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Several states have laws that bar city and county governments from building or running broadband networks, often protecting the private cable and phone companies already operating there. This bill would override those bans, letting states, cities, Indian tribes, and their agencies offer high-speed internet directly or through partnerships. It would also require public providers to treat private competitors fairly, hold a public hearing before starting a network, describe what service low-income areas would get, and give private companies a chance to bid on the project first.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of communities with slow, expensive, or unavailable broadband would gain a new option: their local government could build a public network where private providers have declined to serve or charge high prices. Local governments and Indian tribes would regain the power to decide their own connectivity without state preemption.

how_it_helps.text: No state or local law could prohibit, or have the effect of prohibiting, a public provider — a state, city, tribe, or their agencies — from offering advanced telecommunications capability to anyone [S2][S4].
A public provider that regulates competing providers would have to apply its rules, including rights-of-way and permitting, without favoring itself or its affiliates [S2][S4].

Before launching service, a public provider would have to publish notice, hold a hearing for citizens and businesses, identify any special services for low-income areas, and give private-sector entities 30 days to bid to provide the service instead [S3][S4].
Public providers would be encouraged to consider public-private partnerships before going it alone [S4].

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, incumbent cable, telephone, and broadband companies would face new public competition in markets they currently dominate, and state laws shielding them from municipal rivals would be voided. Taxpayers in participating communities would bear the financial risk if their municipal network failed, though the bill bars federal money for reviving failed projects except in presidentially-declared disaster areas.

drawbacks.text: Municipal broadband projects can fail, leaving local taxpayers covering the loss; the bill itself anticipates this by prohibiting federal funds to revive a project that goes bankrupt or is terminated, except in presidentially-declared major disaster areas [S3][S4].

Private broadband companies argued that government competing against private business is inherently unfair; the bill answers this with anti-discrimination rules, mandatory public hearings, and a 30-day private-bid window, but a public provider still enters the market with tax powers and public assets behind it [S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was written with real concessions to critics: public providers must hold hearings, disclose low-income service plans, accept private bids, treat competitors without discrimination, and cannot expect federal bailouts for failed projects. The main cost falls on incumbent providers facing competition, which is the point of the bill. The main risk is financial failure of a public network, which falls on the locality, not the federal government, by design.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate's calendar of business, but no one ever brought it to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Frank Lautenberg introduced the bill on July 23, 2007, joined by nine senators including both John McCain and Ted Stevens on the Republican side and John Kerry and Russell Feingold on the Democratic side [S1][S4][S6].
It was referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, which ordered it reported favorably with amendments on October 30, 2007 [S6].
On April 22, 2008, the committee reported the bill with amendments and written report No. 110-330 [S3][S6].

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 707) on April 22, 2008 — meaning it was waiting for floor time — and remained there until the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, with no Senate vote ever taken [S1][S6].
The House never acted on companion legislation, so the bill never came close to a floor vote in either chamber [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent cable and broadband companies are better off: the state laws that block municipal broadband competition remain in force, and no community gained a public alternative because the bill died on the calendar without a vote.

for.name: Sen. Frank Lautenberg
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: 8 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support.

for.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
for.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Daniel Inouye (D-HI)
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported favorably with amendments in October 2007 and formally reported it with amendments and written report 110-330 in April 2008.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote after it was placed on the legislative calendar in April 2008.

against.name: Incumbent cable and telephone broadband companies
against.what_they_did: Backed and benefited from the state laws that ban municipal broadband, which this bill would have preempted.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's original sponsors split evenly across party lines — Democrats Lautenberg, Kerry, McCaskill, and Feingold alongside Republicans Smith, McCain, Snowe, and Stevens — and its 8 cosponsors were 4 Republicans and 4 Democrats.

industries.industry: Cable, telephone, and other incumbent broadband providers
industries.note: The bill would void state laws that bar municipal competitors, opening markets these companies currently control to public networks. Their gain from the bill's defeat is the public's continued lack of alternatives in underserved areas.

industries.industry: Local governments and Indian tribes as broadband providers
industries.note: The bill restores their legal ability to build and operate broadband networks for their residents, subject to public-hearing and bidding requirements.

industries.industry: Private broadband contractors and network builders
industries.note: The bill requires a 30-day private-bid window before any public project and encourages public-private partnerships, creating contracting opportunities even as it enables public competition.
